title: Revealing Scaling Paradox in Large-scale Time Series Models: Implications for More Efficient and Accurate Forecasting
claim: Two model families share one input-to-forecast flow, with distinct components for each: fine-tuned pretrained backbones and decoder-only transformers.
layout: 2 stacked panels, left-to-right flow, shared input on left, dashed divider
description: An architecture diagram reading left to right. On the far left, a raw black time series passes through Instance Norm and patching into yellow patch tokens. A prompt box at the top left lists Meta Prompt, Dataset Info, Data Interval, Task Prompt and Statistical Features. These feed into Tokenization, which produces colored prompt token bars. A large rounded gray container holds two stacked panels split by a dashed line. The top panel, LLM4TS, runs TS embedding, then concatenation with the prompt tokens, then a large blue-gray Pre-trained LLM block with a brain icon, a bookshelf icon and the Qwen and OpenAI logos, then a Prediction Head. Flame icons mark the tuned modules. The bottom panel, TSFMs, runs TS embedding, then position embeddings, then a dashed repeated block (×L) of causal self-attention, layer-norm and feed-forward with residual connections, then an Output Layer. Both rows end in Instance De-norm and a forecast curve drawn in red.
caption: Overall structure of our LLM4TS and TSFMs families. Each family consists of four models at different scales. LLM4TS fine-tunes only a small subset of parameters to transfer the extensive knowledge and reasoning capability of LLMs to TS tasks, while incorporating prompts to enhance representation learning. TSFMs adopt a decoder-only architecture that predicts the next token to forecast future.
abstract: Large-scale models are at the forefront of time series (TS) forecasting, dominated by two paradigms: fine-tuning text-based Large Language Models for TS (LLM4TS) and training Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) from scratch. Both approaches share a foundational assumption that scaling up model capacity and data volume leads to improved performance. However, we observe a scaling paradox in TS models, revealing a puzzling phenomenon that larger models do NOT always achieve better performance. Through extensive experiments on two model families across four scales (100M to 1.7B parameters) and diverse data (up to 6B observations), we rigorously confirm that the scaling paradox is a pervasive issue. We then diagnose its root cause by analyzing internal representations, identifying a phenomenon we call few-layer dominance: only a small subset of layers are functionally important, while the majority are redundant, under-utilized, and can even distract training. Based on this discovery, we propose a practical method to automatically identify and retain only these dominant layers. In our models, retaining only 21% of the parameters achieves up to a 12% accuracy improvement and a 2.7x inference speedup. We validate the universality of our method on 8 prominent SOTA models (LLM4TS and TSFMs, 90M to 6B), showing that retaining less than 30% layers achieves superior accuracy in over 95% tasks.
